title: With great joy (Luke 24:50–53)
hook: he blesses them as he's carried up, and they return with great joy
tomorrow: In the beginning was the Word

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last evening in that room: he opened their understanding. Your line was opened. What did you reread and see differently? Day four hundred ninety-one, and the last page of Luke.

How do you say goodbye to someone you will not see again in this life? An airport curb, a hospital bed, a last visit with a grandparent. A goodbye like that can empty a person out: the quiet drive home, the minutes sitting in the car before going inside. Luke's Gospel ends with a goodbye too. But the people in it don't go home quiet. They go home, of all things, with joy. Today we read the last four verses of Luke, and the strange joy at the end of them.
screen: `THE LAST GOODBYE.` → `A QUIET DRIVE HOME.` → `THESE GO HOME WITH JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the ending, in the Douay-Rheims: "And he led them out as far as Bethania: and lifting up his hands, he blessed them." Then, while he is blessing them, he is parted from them and carried up to heaven. His last gesture in this Gospel is a blessing. Hands lifted, the way a priest blesses, and he is still doing it as he goes. And then: "And they adoring went back into Jerusalem with great joy." They had every reason for grief. Instead, joy. Why? Luke has told us. He gave them understanding. He promised power from on high. And he left blessing them, which means the last thing they saw was not his absence but his care. Now look at where Luke ends. In the temple. They were always in the temple, praising and blessing God. Do you remember where this Gospel began, about fifty days ago on this path? In the temple, with an old priest named Zachary, struck silent at the altar, unable to speak to the people waiting outside. Some readers see a frame here: a priest who couldn't speak to the people at the start, and at the end, hands lifted in blessing and people blessing God in return. And between them, the whole Gospel: the angel and Mary, the manger, the boy in the temple, the sermon at Nazareth, the lost and found, the cross, the road to Emmaus. Joy runs through it, from the angel's good tidings of great joy at Bethlehem to this last line. Luke isn't finished, though. He wrote a second volume, the Acts of the Apostles, and it opens by telling the ascension again, more fully, with forty days and a cloud. Catholics celebrate that day as the Ascension of the Lord.
screen: `HE LIFTS HIS HANDS AND BLESSES.` · `THEY RETURN WITH GREAT JOY.` · `IT ENDS WHERE IT BEGAN, THE TEMPLE.` · `LUKE GOES ON IN ACTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: end the day blessing someone. Settle, and breathe. Picture someone you said goodbye to today, even an ordinary goodbye: a kid at school drop-off, a coworker leaving, a parent on the phone. Picture them going on with their evening. Now wish them good, on purpose. Their sleep, their worries, their tomorrow. If you pray, you can ask God to bless them by name. If you don't, just send them the wish. Let the last thing you hold tonight be care, not absence. The bell holds the time.
Bethania. Where Jesus led his disciples, lifted his hands to bless them, and was carried up to heaven, the last page of Luke's story. Today's word.

Your line: great joy. Tonight, make your last word to someone a blessing. And that's the Gospel of Luke, fifty days, from Zachary in the temple to great joy in the temple. Tomorrow, John begins. Day four hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Ascension of the Lord forty days after Easter (moved to the following Sunday in many dioceses), and the Mass ends each time with the priest blessing the people before they are sent out.

original.note: Greek: great joy, the same words the angel uses at Bethlehem (Luke 2:10) and Luke's last note (24:52).

trapdoor: what you thought: the ascension is a sad goodbye.
what it means: he leaves blessing them, and they go home with great joy.
what a scholar hears: Luke opens and closes in the temple, and great joy frames the Gospel from 2:10 to 24:52; Acts 1 retells the ascension with the forty days.

notes: Block D (Luke, days 442–491) closes here; the carry names the block. Confirm whether a fuller look-back is wanted.

Great joy: Luke 2:10 (Greek chara megalē) and 24:52; confirm the Greek form in the original game.
